words.why: A repeated, regular time. Frequency like this is the core of the present simple: I check my email every day.

Both. As a frequency adverb it takes the simple: She always takes the bus. With the continuous it stops being a timetable and becomes a complaint: He’s always interrupting. Same adverb, two grammars, two meanings.
Frequency adverb → present simple. It sits before the main verb: I usually walk.
Frequency adverb → present simple, and the verb stays positive: He never eats meat, not doesn't never.
Frequency adverb → present simple. It is the one that can also open the sentence: Sometimes I walk home.
A repeating appointment. Note the plural -s — that is what makes it every Monday rather than one particular one.
A stated frequency → present simple: She swims twice a week.
Signals a general truth, which is the present simple's other main job: In general, people prefer the direct train.
Frequency adverb → present simple.
Frequency adverb → present simple, and like never it carries the negative itself: I rarely see him.
A repeated season → present simple: They visit every summer.
A more formal way of saying usually → present simple.
This exact moment → present continuous: I'm writing right now.
This moment, or the current stretch of time → present continuous: She's living in Berlin at the moment.
The formal version of at the moment → present continuous: We are currently reviewing your application.
Formal, and points at now → present continuous.
An instruction to look at something happening in front of you → present continuous: Look! It's snowing.
Works exactly like Look! — it points at this second: Listen! Someone's knocking.
As explicit as it gets → present continuous.
An action in progress around another one → present continuous: I'm printing it while you wait.
Both. I have three lessons today is a fact about the timetable — simple. I'm working from home today is a temporary arrangement — continuous. The word does not decide; the meaning does.
Both. The shop closes at six this week (the schedule) against I'm covering for Sam this week (a temporary situation).
Both. Same split as this week: a fixed arrangement takes the simple, a temporary state takes the continuous.
Both. These days people work from home is a general truth — simple. These days I'm cycling in is a temporary change — continuous.
Both, though the simple is far commoner: Nowadays most people book online. The continuous appears for a change still under way.
Both. My birthday falls on a Sunday this year against I'm learning Italian this year.

en.title: Present Simple vs Present Continuous
en.sub: Speed sorting — twenty-six time expressions, three boxes
en.ruleTitle: The rule the game is testing
en.r1n: every day · usually · often · on Mondays · twice a week
en.r2n: right now · at the moment · currently · Look! · Listen!
en.r3n: today, this week, always — a timetable takes the simple, a temporary arrangement takes the continuous, and always with the continuous is a complaint. Seven of the twenty-six belong here.
en.howto: Click a box, drag the card into it, or press 1, 2, 3. You do not have to wait for the card to land.
en.band4: Full marks — including the seven that go either way, which is the hard part.
en.band3: Strong. Check which of the three boxes your misses came from.
en.band2: A fair start. Read the rule card again — especially the third box.
en.band1: Read the rule card, then play again. Everything you need is on it.

de.title: Present Simple vs Present Continuous
de.ruleTitle: Die Regel, um die es im Spiel geht
de.r1n: every day · usually · often · on Mondays · twice a week
de.r2n: right now · at the moment · currently · Look! · Listen!
de.r3b: Manche Ausdrücke passen wirklich zu beidem.
de.r3n: today, this week, always — ein fester Plan verlangt das Simple, eine vorübergehende Regelung das Continuous, und always mit dem Continuous ist eine Beschwerde. Sieben der 26 gehören hierher.
